claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15, Valve's SAPI phoneme extractor (source-sdk-2013 master, src/utils/phonemeextractor/phonemeextractor.cpp, last changed 2025-02-18 in commit 44f8f18; its menu name is "MS SAPI 5.1") does not do free dictation. It runs recognition that is limited by a grammar built from a typed transcript. ExtractPhonemes splits the text on spaces and drops anything inside [ ]. It then builds a dynamic SAPI context-free grammar with one top-level rule, "Root". Each word becomes a state inside that rule (CreateNewState), and word-transition arcs (AddWordTransition) link the states in transcript order. Valve's own comments call these per-word states "rules". The code then turns the grammar on with SetRuleState(NULL, NULL, SPRS_ACTIVE), under the comment "Activate the CFG ( rather than using dictation )", and it never loads a dictation grammar. This is looser than strict forced alignment. When the transcript has more than one word, empty (epsilon) arcs make every word after the first optional. Afterwards, SAPI_ExtractPhonemes puts back any transcript word the recogniser skipped, with its phonemes removed, and ComputeMissingByteSpans spreads such words across the gaps in the timeline. The tool will not run without text. SAPI_ExtractPhonemes prints "Input sentence is empty!", ExtractPhonemes prints "Error:  no rule / text specified", and text that yields no words fails with "contained no usable words". The code runs only on Windows (windows.h, COM/ATL, SAPI 5.1).

As of 2026-09-15, Valve's SAPI phoneme extractor ("MS SAPI 5.1", src/utils/phonemeextractor/phonemeextractor.cpp in ValveSoftware/source-sdk-2013, unchanged since the 2013 first commit) does not acoustically align phoneme boundaries inside a word. The only timing it takes from SAPI is each recognised word's start and end: ulAudioStreamOffset + ullAudioStreamPosition, and that plus ulAudioSizeBytes. SAPI's pszPronunciation supplies which phonemes are in the word. The code then splits the word's span in proportion to fixed per-phoneme weights from the g_Phonemes table in src/public/phonemeconverter.cpp: 0.6 for c/k, 0.7 for y, 0.8 for most stops, fricatives, l and n, 1.0 for most vowels and approximants, and 1.2 for er/er2, ow, uw, ao, aw and oy. An unknown phoneme gets 1.0. The FIXME comment says phonemes are spread evenly, but the code gives them different weights, so the comment is out of date. Words SAPI missed get word spans spread evenly across the gap, with no phonemes. When a word's span is moved (a zero-length word merged with its neighbour, or a gap filled), its phonemes are rescaled in proportion and keep the same relative spacing.

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15: Source engine phoneme (lip-sync) data is stored inside the WAV in a custom RIFF chunk with id 'VDAT' (bytes 56 44 41 54). The id is followed by a 4-byte little-endian length that does not count the 8 id and length bytes, then a whitespace-separated text block. It is not a key-value block. It starts with a 'VERSION 1.0' header, followed by sections in braces: PLAINTEXT { sentence text }; WORDS { WORD <word> <start> <end> { <phoneme code> <phoneme name> <start> <end> <volume, always 1> } ... }; EMPHASIS { <time> <value> ... }; and OPTIONS { voice_duck <0|1> [checksum <n>] }. The reader still skips an old CLOSECAPTION section, but Valve's code marks it 'NO LONGER VALID' and current code never writes it. Only the OPTIONS contents (and the VERSION line) are key-value pairs.

(Checked 2026-09-15) In DMX models, domination rules are DmeCombinationDominationRule elements, held in the DmeCombinationOperator's "dominators" array. Each rule lists "dominators" and "suppressed" names. These are raw control (shape) names, not animator-facing controllers. When the dominating shapes are active, the suppressed shapes fade out. For example, "open jaw" might dominate "puff cheeks". A shape key whose name joins other shape names with underscores ("a_b") is a corrective shape. It fades in additively when all the shapes it is named after are active: a + b applies a_b, and a + b + c applies a_b, a_c, b_c and a_b_c. Because underscores make a shape corrective, don't put underscores in flexes that animators should see. A corrective can name the same shape more than once. "s_s" gives a quadratic response, and further repeats give cubic or quartic ones. Mixing several such shapes at different rates lets one flex controller seem to move vertices along a curved path, even though each flex moves vertices in straight lines.

claims.claim:
As of 2026-09-15, in Source flex animation each flex shape moves its vertices in a straight line from the base position, scaled by the weight. Weights above 1.0 push past the shape and negative weights invert it. Flex controllers do not drive shapes one to one. QC flex rules (*, /, +, -, min, max), DMX DmeFlexRuleExpression, domination rules and corrective shapes (names joined with underscores) combine controller values non-linearly. Corrective shapes can respond quadratically or cubically to one controller, so the path from controller to vertex is not linear. The public Source engine headers set these limits for a compiled model:
- 10,000 flexed vertices per mesh on PC (MAXSTUDIOFLEXVERTS).
- 1,024 flex shapes (MAXSTUDIOFLEXDESC).
- 96 flex controllers (MAXSTUDIOFLEXCTRL).
The headers checked are Source SDK 2013 studio.h and the TF2, L4D2, Alien Swarm, Portal 2 and CS:GO branches. The 96 limit belongs to the compiled model, not to the VTA source format. Vertex offsets are stored as 16-bit fixed-point numbers with a default scale of 1/4096. A vertex can therefore move at most about 8 units on each axis, unless the model header sets its own scale. The Valve Developer Community wiki lists the 8-unit limit under SMD/VTA. The same wiki page (last edited 31 May 2026) says DMX supports 128 flex controllers. No public engine header backs that number, and the page also describes DMX models hitting the 96 limit, so 128 is unverified.
